name: Omar Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm out the door by seven and meet Dev, my boss, at whatever house we're rewiring that week. It's mostly old terraced houses near the river, with cloth-covered cable from the 1960s still in the walls. I lift floorboards, pull new cable, and cut channels in the plaster so the wires can sit flush. Dev does the testing and the paperwork, because I'm still not great at reading the meter results.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment you flip the new board on and every light in the house comes up. I like the people too, the old ladies who make you tea and tell you who lived there before. What wears me out is the dust, my knees, and the feeling that I'm slower than I should be at 27. I failed my licence exam once last spring, and I'm sitting it again in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like the world I'm already in. Dev tried some quoting app last year and went back to his notebook after a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the union branch meeting: the problem was never robots, it's the bosses. Pay for juniors is flat, and rents on our side of town went up again. If AI is just hype, then the fight is the same one we had before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thing that scares me isn't AI, it's that exam. If I fail the licence exam a second time, my boss Dev can hire a cheaper first-year and nobody would blame him. I've got about four months of rent saved, so I'm not on the street, but that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going to the evening revision class at the college every Tuesday. I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, maybe 150, so the cushion doesn't shrink. And I'd keep paying my union dues, because if Dev ever lets me go, the union lawyer is all I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tight in the chest, if I'm honest. Not because of computers. Just because I know I'm the weak link on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the weak link. What happened on the job that makes you feel that way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I wired a kitchen ring and got two cables crossed at the back of a socket. Dev caught it on the test, but he went very quiet. He didn't shout, he just redid it, and that was worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you talk to about that kind of thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lina, my partner, mostly. She works nights at a care home, so we talk in the mornings when she gets in and I'm leaving. She tells me to stop beating myself up, but she also asks if I've done my practice papers.

say: I'd say the **real problem** is low pay for juniors, not robots.
I'd tell the **union branch** the fight about wages and rent is the same as before.
think: I think my **licence exam** in March matters far more than any AI.
I fear Dev could **replace me** with a cheaper first-year if I fail again.
do: Keep going to the **Tuesday revision class** at the college until the March exam.
Put aside about **150 a month** to keep four months of rent saved.
Keep paying **union dues** so I have legal help if I'm let go.
feel: I feel **tight in the chest** about being the weakest one on the crew.
S0.quote: If I fail the licence exam a second time, my boss Dev can hire a cheaper first-year and nobody would blame him.
fieldNote: Omar's worry in the calm scenario is his **own skill**, not technology.
He has a **four-month cushion** and a partner earning, which softens the risk.
He trusts the **union** more than his boss as a safety net.

steps.text: Resit the electrician's licence exam in March after weekly revision classes
Save about 150 a month towards the rent cushion
Keep paying union dues and stay on the branch mailing list

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and booking and answering customers, that's Dev's side, not mine. My side is floorboards and cable, and no software lifts a floorboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to the app that tries to crawl into a loft in August. Online I'd probably share something about the call centre jobs going, because Lina's sister answers phones for an energy company and she'd be in the firing line. I'd say the government should make firms pay for the people they drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it mostly means Dev gets his evenings back, because the quoting and the certificates get done by a program. My boss doing his paperwork faster won't lift a single floorboard, so my knees are still safe. The bit that bothers me is if the test results get read by a machine, then my weak spot matters less, and maybe that's actually good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, mostly: pass the exam, keep saving. I'd go to the union's meetings about AI if they ran any, because I'd want rules on how firms use it. I won't put an app on my phone, I'm not changing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for other people more than for me. It's like watching rain on the other side of the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a machine reading the test results might help you. Would you use it if Dev asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Dev made it part of the job, I'd do it, I'm not going to lose my place over an app. But I'd want him to show me twice. Last time he showed me the meter's Bluetooth thing, I pressed the wrong button and wiped a whole morning of readings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Lina's sister? What would you say to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to get into the union now, before the cuts, not after. She'd roll her eyes. She thinks unions are for old men in hard hats.

say: I'd say the **call centre jobs** go first, not the hands-on trades.
I'd say firms should **pay for the people** they drop.
think: I think **software** takes Dev's paperwork, while floorboards and cable stay with me.
I quietly hope a machine reading **test results** covers my weak spot.
do: Keep revising for the **licence exam** and saving each month.
Go to any **union meetings** about rules for AI at work.
Refuse to install **apps** unless Dev makes one part of the job.
feel: I feel **uneasy for others**, like rain on the far side of the valley.
S1.quote: My boss doing his paperwork faster won't lift a single floorboard, so my knees are still safe.
fieldNote: Omar sees the **thinking work** as Dev's, so feels shielded in this scenario.
His **fear of apps** comes from one specific mistake with the meter.
He pushes **unions** on family before taking any step himself.

steps.text: Keep up weekly revision for the March licence exam
Ask the union branch to run a meeting on AI rules at work
Wait for Dev to bring in any new testing app before touching it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking stuff, five for robots. That's before I'd even finish paying off the van I want to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the state to step in: a tax on the firms using it and money for the people pushed out. I'd say it loud at the branch. I'd probably post about it too, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the first thing to go is my bit, not Dev's. A robot that can pull cable through a loft is coming for the junior, not for the man who signs the certificate. By 2031 I'd be 32 and still the slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop thinking about the van and pile everything into savings, maybe 300 a month instead of 150. I'd push the union to fight for a rule that a licensed person has to sign off every job, robot or not. And I'd really, really try to pass that exam, because the licence is the only thing a robot can't hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, to be honest. Like the floor is going and I'm standing on the joists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lina the night you heard this was real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not having the talk about moving in together properly yet, the bigger flat, until we see what's left of my job. She'd say her care job is safe because robots can't comfort someone at 3 a.m. Maybe she's right, and then she'd be carrying us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you don't want to use apps or AI. In this picture, does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hate to say it, but probably not. I know I should learn it, but I'd rather spend the time making sure my hands are better than anyone's. It's stubborn, I know.

say: I'd say the **state must step in** with a tax on firms using it.
I'd speak up at the **union branch** and even post online.
think: I think the **junior's work** goes to robots before the boss's signature does.
I fear being 32 and still the **slowest one** when robots arrive in 2031.
do: Double my **savings to 300** a month and drop the van plan.
Push the union for a **licensed sign-off** rule on every job.
Pass the **licence exam**, the one thing a robot can't hold.
feel: I feel **scared**, like the floor is gone and I'm standing on joists.
S2.quote: A robot that can pull cable through a loft is coming for the junior, not for the man who signs the certificate.
fieldNote: Omar spots that the robot wave hits **junior hands-on work** first, which flips his earlier calm.
He still **won't learn AI**, and says plainly that it's stubborn.
Lina's **care job** becomes the household's fallback in his mind.

steps.text: Drop the van purchase and save 300 a month
Campaign at the union for a licensed sign-off on every job
Put off moving to a bigger flat with Lina
Pass the licence exam in March

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots by 2034. That's a bit more like a plan and less like a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said with the fast one: the people building this should pay into a fund for the trades. Five years is enough time for governments to sort something out if they want to. I'd say that at the branch, and I'd vote for whoever promises it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gets me the licence and some real experience, which matters. By 2034 I'd be 35 with a licence, and a licence plus ten years of old houses counts for something. But I still think the cable-pulling jobs dry up for the young lads behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pass the exam, then ask Dev to start teaching me the testing and inspection side properly, because that's signing work. I'd save, but not panic-save, maybe 200 a month. I'd join the union's campaign group, not just pay dues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a worry I can work with. Not a scream, more a hum in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd vote for whoever promises a fund. What would you need to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see real numbers, not speeches. Like, if you're pushed out of the trade at 33, you get a year's pay and a free course. My dad lost his factory job in his forties and got nothing but a leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to work alongside the robots, if that's what keeps you in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the union got a deal where the electrician runs the robot and keeps the pay, then yes, I'd learn it. But only with that deal. On my own, I don't trust myself with the tech.

say: I'd say AI firms should pay into a **fund for the trades**.
I'd say five years is **enough time** for governments to act.
think: I think five years gets me **licensed** with real experience behind me.
I still think **cable-pulling jobs** dry up for the juniors behind me.
do: Pass the exam and ask Dev to teach me **testing and inspection**.
Save about **200 a month** without panic.
Join the union's **campaign group**, not just pay dues.
feel: I feel a **steady worry**, more a hum than a scream.
S3.quote: By 2034 I'd be 35 with a licence, and a licence plus ten years of old houses counts for something.
fieldNote: The extra three years let Omar picture a **licence plus experience**, which steadies him.
His father's **factory layoff** shapes his demand for real numbers, not speeches.
He'd learn robot work only under a **union deal**.

steps.text: Ask Dev to teach testing and inspection after passing the licence exam
Join the union's campaign group on AI and the trades
Vote for candidates who promise a retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. By 2039 for the robots, I'd be 40. That's half a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it. I'd tell the branch we should use it to write rules now, not when the robots are in the van. Online I'd say the same, if I said anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine for most of it, and then it gets hard right when I should be earning the most. Ten years is long enough to get good at this trade and short enough to lose it at forty. That's the bit I'd chew on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pass the licence, get five or six years in, then look at getting the inspector's qualification, because that's the paperwork side that needs a signature. I'd keep saving 150 a month. And I'd stay in the union and maybe stand for branch committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but still uneasy. It's like knowing the landlord is going to sell, just not this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might stand for the branch committee. What's stopping you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly that I'm shy in meetings, and I'm the youngest there by fifteen years. Raymond, the branch secretary, keeps asking. Maybe in ten years I'd finally say yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The inspector's work is more paperwork and thinking. Doesn't the AI arrive there first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, you're right, and I hadn't thought of that. Maybe the bit that lasts is being the person who's legally responsible, whatever does the work. I'd need the union to make sure that stays a human job.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift we shouldn't waste.
I'd say the union should **write the rules now**, not later.
think: I think the hard part lands at **forty**, when I should be earning most.
I'd be **fine for most** of the decade.
do: Pass the licence and plan an **inspector's qualification** after five or six years.
Keep saving **150 a month** as before.
feel: I feel **calmer but uneasy**, like a landlord selling up, just not this year.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to get good at this trade and short enough to lose it at forty.
fieldNote: Omar sees the danger landing at his **peak earning years**, not now.
He noticed mid-answer that **inspection is thinking work** too, and shifted to legal responsibility.
His **shyness** is the real barrier to taking a union role.

steps.text: Plan to take the inspector's qualification after five or six licensed years
Tell Raymond at the branch he'll stand for committee

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because the robots would get here while I'm still the slow junior. What would help is a rule that a licensed electrician signs off every job, and a proper fund, a year's pay and a course, if you're pushed out. My dad got a leaflet when his factory shut, and I don't want a leaflet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the exam. Everyone thinks the threat is the robot. For me, this year, the threat is a multiple-choice paper in March.

headlineQuote: My dad got a leaflet when his factory shut, and I don't want a leaflet.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old junior** rewiring old terraced houses with his boss Dev.
He failed his **licence exam** once and resits in March; that worries him more than AI.
He trusts the **union** and the state, and refuses to use apps or AI.
He grows **alarmed** when robots could arrive while he's still junior, and steadier with more time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive while he's still the slow junior.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that a **licensed electrician signs off** every job.
A **fund paying** a year’s wages and a course for anyone pushed out.
